# The Strange Comfort of Rain

I've been thinking about why rain feels like permission. Permission to slow down, to cancel plans without guilt, to sit inside with a book and let the world soften outside the window. There's something about weather that takes the blame off us—we're not lazy if it's raining, we're just sensible.

But I think it's more than that. Rain is democratic. It falls on everyone equally, regardless of how productive they've been. On a rainy day, the CEO and the unemployed person are experiencing the same grey sky. There's an odd equality in that.

I also love that rain makes people honest. Nobody's pretending they're having a great day when it's pouring. You don't run into a rainy day and fake-smile about it. You just accept it. And there's relief in that—in a world that constantly asks us to spin negative things positively, rain says: "No, this is gloomy, and that's okay."

The sound is probably doing half the work. Rain is one of the few ambient sounds we're evolutionarily wired to find soothing. It masks other noises, creates white noise, signals that predators probably aren't hunting right now. We can rest.

Maybe what we're really craving when we love rainy days isn't the rain itself—it's permission. Permission to exist without performing, to feel what we feel, to be still. 

We should probably give ourselves that permission more often, regardless of the weather.
